title: Switched-Capacitor Circuits
intro: Switched-capacitor (SC) circuits look at their input only at clock instants and process each sample with capacitors, switches and an op amp. CMOS suits them perfectly: MOS switches pass signals with no offset and MOS gates draw no current, so a stored charge stays put (Razavi, Chapter 13).

blocks.text: A CMOS op amp gets its gain from a high output resistance, so a resistive feedback network loads it and spoils the precision of a resistor-ratio gain. Capacitors draw no DC current once the output has settled, and on-chip capacitor ratios match to about 0.1%. The catch is that a capacitive network leaves the op-amp input node without a DC path, so switches are needed to reset and bias it; this makes the circuit discrete-time, working in a sampling phase and an amplification (or integration) phase.

blocks.alt: Schematic. Vin passes through switch S1 to node P, which connects through capacitor C1 to node X, the minus input of an op amp whose plus input is grounded. Switch S3 connects P to ground. Capacitor C2 and switch S2 each connect X to the output.
blocks.caption: The basic SC amplifier: sample $V_{in}$ on $C_1$, then transfer the charge to $C_2$.

items: SC Fundamentals: resistive versus capacitive feedback, the reset switch, sampling and amplification phases, charge transfer.
Sampling Switches: the MOS switch as a sampler, on-resistance against signal level, speed, complementary switches.
Switch Precision: charge injection, clock feedthrough, $kT/C$ noise and ways to cancel the errors.
Switched-Capacitor Amplifiers: the unity-gain sampler, the non-inverting amplifier and the multiply-by-two circuit, with their gain errors and time constants.
SC Integrators and Common-Mode Feedback: the switched-capacitor resistor, integrators that ignore parasitics, and SC CMFB.

blocks.text: Two habits pay off throughout: track charge, not voltage, at nodes that float (no resistive path to anything), and arrange the clock so the switch that sets the sampling instant is the one whose charge injection does not depend on the signal.

blocks.title: Gain from a capacitor ratio
blocks.text: An SC amplifier uses $C_1 = 3$ pF and $C_2 = 0.75$ pF. A 0.2 V input is sampled. What is the ideal output after amplification, and what happens to the output if $C_1$ and $C_2$ are both 5% larger than drawn?
solution: Both scale together, so the ratio, and the output, are unchanged: only mismatch between them matters.
